newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Goldman Sachs urges tough action on Thai baht.
newsitem.headline: Goldman Sachs urges tough action on Thai baht.

text.p: Thailand must raise interest rates and come up with a credible plan to deal with the asset quality problems plaguing its financial system if it wants to stabilise the baht, Goldman Sachs has warned.

"This means shutting down insolvent institutions and building the capital base of viable ones. The longer the delay in formulating such a plan, the greater will be the baht's susceptibility to speculative attacks," the U.S. investment bank said in a recent report.

Although Goldman Sachs considers the baht fairly valued within its current range against a basket of currencies dominated by the U.S. dollar, it has raised its probability of a devaluation to 25 percent within three months from five percent one month ago.
The baht has been trading at 6-1/2 year highs of 26.01 against the strengthening U.S. dollar.
Overnight rates are soaring, reaching 26 percent during the traditionally tight liquidity days of Lunar New Year before they settled back this week to about 13 percent.
Precipitating the crisis were a much-worse-than-expected fiscal balance in the fourth quarter of 1996 and speculation of default by a major finance company.

Government revelations of an expected fiscal deficit in the fourth quarter prompted concern about financing arrangements for Thailand's widening current account deficit against a backdrop of mounting economic malaise.
In the past 10 days:
* Property developer Somprasong Lang Plc defaulted on a Euroconvertible debenture payment;
* Finance One Plc denied persistent market rumours last week that it was in financial difficulty.
* The central bank was criticised for its bailout of Bangkok Bank of Commerce.
The Thai government continues to deny any rumours of a devaulation while defending the baht aggressively.

The recent woes follow months of nervousness due to a huge current account deficit, deteriorating asset quality in the financial sector due to an oversupply of property and high interest rates in the midst of an economic downturn.

Goldman Sachs said the key to the asset quality problems was massive rates of credit expansion throughout the early 1990s. Loans are estimated to reach 144 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) at the end of 1996 compared with 90 percent in 1991.

Non-performing loans in finance companies, heavily geared to the troubled property sector, are now estimated at 20 percent. Non-performing loans at banks are believed to be about 9.8 percent and are forecast to rise to 14 percent, Goldman said.

Compounding these difficulties are foreign liabilities following the BIBF, or Bangkok International Banking Facility, system, which boosted total foreign liability in Thai banks to more than 23 percent.

"As a result, foreign investors' assessment of the health of the banking system has become a key parameter determining the strength of capital inflows and hence the financeability of the country's current account deficit," Goldman said.

If non-performing loans peak at 15 percent as expected, and 30 percent of those loans are unrecoverable, the total loss will amount to about US$10.5 billion, or roughly 38 percent of the existing equity of the financial system and six percent of GDP, Goldman Sachs said.
"This is a large, but manageable amount if one considers losses could also be allocated to the government and/or depositors as well as the banks' shareholders," Goldman said.

Goldman Sachs has also revised its estimate for 1997 GDP to five percent from 6.2 percent in response to slowing revenues. The current account deficit is expected to widen to eight percent of GDP, it said.
